misconception_description: Student believes that conditional statements, i.e., Python statements that evaluate to either True or False, must be explicitly compared to True or False to be used in conditionals.

solutions.generated_code:
program MatriksIdentitas
kamus
  n, i, j : integer
  baris : string
algoritma
  input(n)
  for i <- 1 to n do
    baris <- ""
    for j <- 1 to n do
      if (i == j) == true then
        baris <- baris + "1 "
      else
        baris <- baris + "0 "
      endif
    endfor
    output(baris)
  endfor
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: Rewrote the solution to use a more straightforward nested loop approach that checks if the row index equals the column index. Applied the misconception by explicitly comparing (i == j) to True, even though i == j already evaluates to a boolean. The student believes this explicit comparison is necessary for the conditional to work properly. The code functions correctly despite the redundant comparison, making this a benign misconception.
